app.title: Extreme Weather Safety Quiz
app.intro: Floods, heatwaves and thunderstorms are becoming more frequent in Switzerland. Pick a scenario, answer three questions and learn what the official guidance says.
app.disclaimer: Demo content written for this portfolio project, based on official Swiss guidance. In an emergency, always follow official warnings and instructions.

results.good: Good job! Review the tips below to close the gaps.
results.low: Worth a second look. The official tips below explain what to do.

scenarios.title: Flooding
scenarios.description: Rising rivers, flooded streets and basements: what keeps you safe when the water comes?

questions.situation: Heavy rain has been falling for hours. A flood warning has been issued for your town and water is starting to collect in the street. Your car is parked in the building's underground car park.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Go down quickly and drive the car to higher ground
Stay out of the underground car park and the basement
Go to the basement to switch off the electricity
Wait inside the car park until the rain stops
questions.explanation: Underground spaces can fill with water within minutes, and you can become trapped. When there is a danger of flooding, the official advice is clear: do not enter basements or underground car parks. Moving cars and valuables is something to do earlier, when a flood is first announced, not once the water is rising.

sources.label: Natural Hazards Portal: General recommendations for floods

questions.situation: On your way to class by bike, the road ahead is covered with fast-flowing water. It looks only ankle-deep.
questions.question: What do you do?
options: Ride through quickly, it's shallow
Push the bike through carefully
Turn back and take another route
Follow the car in front of you through the water
questions.explanation: Moving water is stronger than it looks and can hide a damaged road surface, open drains or debris. Official guidance says not to drive or cycle on flooded roads and to keep away from rivers and lakes carrying floodwater, because their banks can collapse.

sources.label: Natural Hazards Portal: General recommendations for floods

questions.situation: Authorities expect a flood in your neighbourhood tomorrow. You live in a ground-floor flat with a cellar.
questions.question: Which preparation makes the most sense today?
options: Move valuables out of the cellar and get sandbags or sealing material ready
Do nothing until the water actually arrives
Open the cellar windows so the water can drain away
Store fuel and chemicals in the cellar so they're out of the way
questions.explanation: When a flood is announced, move mobile valuables (car, furniture) to a safe place, cut the power and gas in rooms at risk, and seal openings with prepared material without putting yourself in danger. Keep polluting or flammable substances out of areas that may flood, and check whether neighbours need help.

scenarios.title: Heatwaves
scenarios.description: Hot days and tropical nights put your health at risk. Do you know how to stay cool and help others?

questions.situation: A heatwave is forecast for the whole week and you want to keep up your running training.
questions.question: When is the best time to run?
options: At midday, so your body gets used to the heat
Early in the morning or late in the evening
Mid-afternoon, after lunch
Any time, as long as you drink afterwards
questions.explanation: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) advises avoiding strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day, from the midday sun (11 a.m. to 3 p.m.) to the high temperatures that follow (3 p.m. to 5 p.m.). Move training to early morning or late evening, and drink regularly: at least 1.5 litres a day.

sources.label: FOPH: Protecting yourself and others in hot weather

questions.situation: Your student flat gets very hot during the heatwave and you have no air conditioning.
questions.question: What is the best way to keep it cool?
options: Keep the windows wide open all day for a breeze
Close windows and shutters during the day, and air the flat at night and early in the morning
Leave your computer and TV on standby so they're ready
Keep the blinds open to let in natural light
questions.explanation: Keep the heat out during the day: close the windows and cover them with external shutters or blinds. Open the windows at night and early in the morning, when it's cooler outside than inside, and switch off devices you don't need.

sources.label: FOPH: Protecting yourself and others in hot weather
Natural Hazards Portal: General recommendations for heatwaves

questions.situation: On a hot afternoon you notice that your older neighbour, who lives alone, seems confused and dizzy.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Let them rest alone; it will pass
Offer them a strong coffee or an alcoholic drink
Cool them with damp towels, give them a drink, and call a doctor or 144 if they don't feel better soon
Take them for a walk outside for some fresh air
questions.explanation: Confusion and dizziness can be signs of heat-related illness. The FOPH advises cooling down with damp towels and drinking something with electrolytes, such as diluted apple juice. If the person doesn't feel better after a short time, call a doctor or 144 (ambulance). Older people who live alone are at higher risk, so check on them during heatwaves.

scenarios.title: Severe thunderstorms
scenarios.description: Lightning, hail and sudden gusts can arrive within minutes. Know what to do outdoors and on the lake.

questions.situation: You're hiking in the hills when you see a flash of lightning. You count 6 seconds until you hear the thunder.
questions.question: Roughly how far away is the storm?
options: About 6 km
About 2 km
About 18 km
Too far away to worry about
questions.explanation: Divide the seconds between the lightning and the thunder by three to get the distance in kilometres: 6 ÷ 3 = about 2 km. That is very close, so look for shelter immediately.

sources.label: Natural Hazards Portal: General recommendations for thunderstorms

questions.situation: The storm is right above you and there is no building nearby.
questions.question: Where are you safest?
options: Under a large, isolated tree
On the ridge, so you can watch the storm
In a car, or else crouched low in open terrain
Lying flat on the ground
questions.explanation: Official advice is to seek shelter in a building or a car. In open terrain with lightning nearby, take a crouched position. Avoid isolated trees, summits and ridges, and also flooded roads, riverbeds and steep slopes.

sources.label: Natural Hazards Portal: General recommendations for thunderstorms

questions.situation: You're on a stand-up paddleboard on a Swiss lake. The orange warning lights on the shore start flashing about 90 times per minute.
questions.question: What does this mean?
options: The lake is closed for a regatta
Storm warning: get off the water immediately
Strong-wind caution: it's fine to stay out a little longer
The swimming area is closing for the day
questions.explanation: Swiss lakes have a storm warning service run by MeteoSwiss. About 40 flashes per minute is a strong-wind warning (gusts of about 46–61 km/h): watch the weather closely. About 90 flashes per minute is a storm warning (gusts above about 61 km/h): take safety measures immediately and head for shore.

sources.label: MeteoSwiss: Storm warning service for Swiss lakes (PDF, German)
